In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the hepatic receptors for PRL in rats during the course of ID or neuroleptic treatment.
the effects of ID on the dopaminergic activity of the brain and its possible role in the induction of the PRL receptors.
the role of the endogenous PRL and its receptors in the development of hepatic steatosis in rats with iron deficiency.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

ID and neuroleptic treatment induce PRL binding sites in the liver, that these binding sites are similar to classical PRL receptors and that the induction of these sites by ID and neuroleptices is additive.
ID and chronic neuroleptic treatment result in a significant increase in the number of high affinity PRL receptors in the liver, and that the mechanism of this increase is not yet known.
the PRL receptor induction by ID and neuroleptical treatment may be a result of the increased PRL levels and/or the reduced dopamine levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neuroleptics (haloperidol, fluphenazine, and chlorpromazine) and nutritional iron deficiency (ID) induce PRL receptors in the rat liver.
ID and neuroleptices increase hepatic PRL receptor number, but not PRL binding affinity.
the PRL receptors are induced by ID and by neuroleptics, and the mechanism of induction is probably mediated through a common pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that

iron deficiency is a common nutritional problem that affects millions of people worldwide, and it can be a risk factor for the development of many health complications, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders.

iron deficiency is a common nutritional deficiency that is not only associated with anemia but also with a number of neurologic and psychiatric symptoms, which may be related to the increased prolactin receptors.
